column1: Why are heat breaks never manufactured from aluminum despite its superior machinability?
column2: Aluminum 6061 has thermal conductivity ~205 W/m·K vs stainless steel 304's ~16 W/m·K—a 13x difference. A heat break must have LOW conductivity to maintain a sharp thermal gradient; aluminum would conduct heat into the cold end, causing heat creep and filament jamming.

column1: What is the key rheological difference between semi-crystalline and amorphous thermoplastics in FDM extrusion?
column2: Semi-crystalline polymers (PLA, PA, PEEK) have a sharp melting transition—viscosity drops by orders of magnitude within a narrow thermal band at Tm. Amorphous polymers (ABS, PETG, PC) soften gradually through Tg into a rubbery plateau with no discrete melting point, giving smoother, more forgiving viscosity-temperature behavior.

column1: What happens if PLA is extruded at 185°C vs 230°C?
column2: At 185°C: unmelted crystallites remain, risking nozzle jams (below effective melt viscosity threshold). At 230°C: viscosity drops too far, causing excessive oozing and stringing.

column1: State Fourier's law for heat flux through the heat break and define each term.
column2: q = -kA(dT/dx), where q = heat flux, k = thermal conductivity, A = cross-sectional area, dT/dx = temperature gradient along the tube length.

column1: What is the formula for thermal resistance through a cylindrical heat break section, and what design implication does it reveal?
column2: R = L/(kA). It reveals that increasing length (L) or decreasing cross-sectional area (A) increases thermal resistance, improving the thermal break's isolation of the heater block from the cold end.

column1: Why must the hotend's melt zone and cold end have contradictory thermal designs?
column2: The melt zone needs high thermal mass to prevent temperature droop during high-flow extrusion, while the cold end must keep filament below Tg to maintain drive-gear grip. A sharp thermal break (heat break) reconciles these opposing requirements.

column1: What is the core kinematic difference between CoreXY and standard Cartesian motion systems?
column2: CoreXY uses two crossed belts where both motors are frame-mounted and stationary; motor A forward + motor B reverse = pure X motion, both motors same direction = pure Y motion. This isolates heavy actuators from the toolhead, unlike Cartesian systems where axis motors move with their respective carriages/bed.

column1: Why does a Cartesian 'bed-slinger' printer suffer asymmetric inertial loading between X and Y axes?
column2: The Y-axis must accelerate the heavy build plate (bed), while the X-axis only moves the lightweight toolhead/carriage—creating a large disparity in achievable acceleration between the two axes.

column1: What mechanism governs interlayer (Z-axis) strength in FDM, and what kinetic law describes it?
column2: Polymer chain diffusion ('healing') across the interface, which requires both layers to be above Tg for chain mobility. It follows Fickian kinetics: diffusion depth is proportional to the square root of time the interface remains above Tg.

column1: Why are FDM parts fundamentally anisotropic rather than isotropic like injection-molded parts?
column2: Because Z-axis strength depends on polymer chain diffusion/healing between layers (a distinct, weaker process from bulk melting within a single extruded line), creating directional-dependent mechanical properties unlike homogeneous injection-molded solids.

column1: What causes warping and delamination in FDM prints, mechanistically?
column2: Differential thermal contraction: upper layers cool/shrink and pull inward on layers below (residual stress). If bed adhesion is insufficient to resist this bending moment, the part warps; if adhesion holds but stress exceeds interlayer tensile strength, the part delaminates.

column1: What happens if the interface between two FDM layers cools too rapidly before chain diffusion completes?
column2: The polymer chains never intermingle across the interface, leaving a distinct weld line that acts as a stress concentration point, weakening interlayer (Z-axis) tensile strength.
